selection_policy: Every record is verified absent from the main super-2.0 dataset under its canonical spelling, documented Romanized variants, and exact Arabic script form.

Complete de-duplication verified across all 6,532+ existing records in the repository.
Suppresses lucky attributes, astrology, and personality divination; localized translations are scholarly drafts requiring native review.

names.name: Qatadah
names.morphology: Classical Arabic substantive noun from the qatad tree (tragacanth), denoting a hardy, enduring desert shrub with thorny resilience, symbolizing steadfast fortitude.
names.short_meaning: Hardy enduring plant; companion Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man al-Ansari.
names.primary_meaning: Qatadah (قَتَادَة) is an authentic Arabic masculine name meaning 'hardy, resilient plant' or 'symbol of enduring steadfastness'. In Islamic history, it is the renowned name of Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man al-Ansari, a heroic companion present at Badr whose eye was struck at Uhud and miraculously healed by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.
names.literal_meaning: A single tree or stem of qatad (a resilient thorny desert shrub), representing patience, rugged strength, and endurance.
names.meaning_explanation: The root q-t-d refers to the resilient desert plant celebrated in classical Arabic poetry for its perseverance in arid climates. As a personal name, Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man was an early convert from the Aws tribe who defended the Prophet ﷺ at the Battle of Uhud. During the battle, his eye was struck out of its socket; the Prophet ﷺ set it back in place with his hand and supplicated, whereupon it became his sharper and better eye.
names.semantic_domain: Resilience, miracle of healing, Badr, companion name

quranic.note: Qatadah is not mentioned in the Qur'an; its Islamic veneration is founded in authentic hadith and Sahaba biography.

hadith_status.note: The healing of Qatadah's eye at Uhud is recorded in Dalā'il al-Nubuwwah by al-Bayhaqi and documented in Al-Isabah (Entry 7076).

prophetic_status.note: Not the name of a prophet; it is the name of a venerated Companion.

companion_status.note: Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man al-Ansari (d. 23 AH / 644 CE), veteran of Badr, Uhud, and the Trench, whose funeral prayer was led by Caliph Umar.

names.religion_association: Heroic early Muslim companion; veteran of Badr and Uhud
names.religious_status: Name of an esteemed Sahabi praised for valor and personal sacrifice in defense of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.

names.cultural_note: A timeless name across the Arab world and Islamic scholarly history, also borne by the famous early Quranic commentator Qatadah ibn Di'amah al-Sadusi.
names.cultural_interpretation: Chosen to inspire enduring patience, resilience in trial, physical and moral bravery, and dedication to faith.
names.usage_note: A respected, classical masculine name consistently documented in historical biographical chronicles and contemporary civil registers.

names.name: Tamadur
names.morphology: Classical Arabic proper feminine noun (pattern tumāḍir) derived from maḍura, denoting milk-white radiance, purity, and sweetness of character.
names.short_meaning: Radiant purity, brilliant white; celebrated female companion and poetess al-Khansa.
names.primary_meaning: Tamadur (تُمَاضِر) is an illustrious Arabic feminine given name meaning 'radiant, luminous white', 'she who possesses pure clarity', or 'sweet-natured'. In Islamic history, it is the renowned personal name of Tamadur bint Amr ibn al-Harith, universally famous by her title al-Khansa'—the greatest poetess of classical Arabia who embraced Islam and whose four sons were martyred at al-Qadisiyyah.
names.literal_meaning: Derived from al-maḍīr (pure white milk that is wholesome and sweet), signifying brightness, noble beauty, and untainted character.
names.meaning_explanation: The root m-ḍ-r in Arabic signifies white radiance and sweet wholesomeness. As a historical name, Tamadur bint Amr was born into the noble Banu Sulaym tribe. She accepted Islam before the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, who admired her eloquence. At the Battle of al-Qadisiyyah, she sent her four sons into the fray with fiery exhortations; when all four fell as martyrs, she did not wail as in pre-Islamic times, but prostrated and thanked God for honoring her with their martyrdom.
names.semantic_domain: Eloquence, patience, maternal sacrifice, Sahabiyyah name

quranic.note: Tamadur does not appear in the Quran; its Islamic resonance is founded on the Sahabiyyah's celebrated conversion and heroic patience.

hadith_status.note: Documented in Ibn Abd al-Barr's Al-Isti'ab and Al-Isabah (Entry 11005) recounting her audience with the Prophet ﷺ and her speech to her sons at al-Qadisiyyah.

prophetic_status.note: Not a prophet's name; it is the personal name of a distinguished female companion (Sahabiyyah).

names.cultural_note: Revered across the Arab and Muslim world as the premier female literary genius of classical Arabic history and an archetype of Muslim womanhood.
names.cultural_interpretation: Chosen to inspire brilliant eloquence, emotional resilience, profound dignity, and deep maternal devotion.

names.primary_meaning: Rumaytha (رُمَيْثَة) is a delicate Arabic feminine given name meaning 'a fragrant desert blossom' or 'gentle, sweet-scented plant'. In Islamic history, it is the renowned name of Rumaytha bint Amr al-Ansariyyah, a noble female companion who sat in the presence of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and narrated the famous description of the Seal of Prophethood.
names.literal_meaning: Diminutive form of ramth (a sweet-scented desert shrub), conveying affectionate grace, resilience, and pleasant fragrance.
names.meaning_explanation: The root r-m-th refers to the flowering desert shrub ramth known for its pleasant scent and resilience in Arabian soil. Rumaytha bint Amr was an early Ansari companion from Medina. She was so close to the Prophet's assembly that she reported hearing his words distinctly and seeing the physical Seal of Prophethood (Khatam al-Nubuwwah) between his shoulder blades.

names.name: Muadhah
names.morphology: Classical Arabic passive participle / noun of protection (pattern mufāʿalah / muʿādhah) from ʿādha, meaning 'she who is sheltered by God's divine refuge and protection'.
names.short_meaning: Divinely protected, sheltered by God; famed early scholar Mu'adhah al-Adawiyyah.
names.primary_meaning: Muadhah (مُعَاذَة) is an Arabic feminine given name meaning 'she who is granted divine refuge', 'protected by God', or 'safeguarded from harm'. In Islamic history, it is the renowned name of Mu'adhah bint Abdillah al-Adawiyyah, the illustrious female scholar, ascetic, and senior hadith narrator who studied directly under Aisha and Ali ibn Abi Talib.
names.literal_meaning: Placed under divine sanctuary and refuge (isti'ādhah), preserved by Allah from spiritual and worldly tribulations.
names.meaning_explanation: The root ʿ-w-dh is the basis of seeking refuge in God from all evil (as in Surah al-Falaq and Surah an-Nas). Mu'adhah al-Adawiyyah of Basra was revered as one of the most brilliant and pious women in the early Islamic generation (Tabi'at). Her narrations are accepted in the six canonical collections (al-Kutub al-Sittah) including Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim.
names.semantic_domain: Divine protection, scholarship, hadith transmission, piety

quranic.note: The personal name Muadhah is not in the Qur'an; its triliteral root ʿ-w-dh forms the foundation of the sacred Qur'anic refuge formula (e.g. 113:1, 114:1).

hadith_status.note: Documented throughout Sahih al-Bukhari (321) and Sahih Muslim (335) as a primary authority narrating legal rulings from Aisha.

names.name: Namariq

names.short_meaning: Silk cushions of Paradise; directly attested Qur'anic term.
names.primary_meaning: Namariq (نَمَارِق) is a Qur'anic feminine given name meaning 'luxurious cushions of Paradise' or 'pillows of celestial serenity'. It is directly attested in the Holy Qur'an in Surah al-Ghashiyah (88:15) depicting the sublime comfort, honor, and beauty prepared for the righteous in the eternal gardens.
names.literal_meaning: Plural of numruqah (a soft, elegant cushion or pillow of rich silk), signifying peaceful repose, dignity, and elevated comfort.
names.meaning_explanation: In Surah al-Ghashiyah (88:15), Allah describes the blessings of Jannah: 'وَنَمَارِقُ مَصْفُوفَةٌ' ('And cushions arrayed in ranks'). Classical commentators including Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi explain that namariq are cushions of vibrant silk lined up side by side for the believers to recline upon in joyful contemplation, symbolizing peace and honor.
names.semantic_domain: Paradise, celestial comfort, serenity, Quranic term

quranic.note: Directly attested in the Qur'an in Surah al-Ghashiyah (88:15): وَنَمَارِقُ مَصْفُوفَةٌ.

hadith_status.note: Referred to in hadiths describing the furnishings and reclining assemblies of the people of Paradise (e.g. Musnad Ahmad 2145).

names.primary_meaning: Jandab (جُنْدَب) is an authentic Arabic masculine given name meaning 'agile, energetic mover' or 'resilient desert champion'. In Islamic history, it is the renowned personal name of the heroic early companion Abu Dharr al-Ghifari (Jandab ibn Junadah), celebrated for uncompromised truthfulness, as well as Jandab ibn Abdillah al-Bajali.
names.literal_meaning: A classical Arabic name representing energetic alertness, swift motion, and unyielding self-reliance in the open desert.
names.meaning_explanation: Jandab ibn Junadah al-Ghifari was the fourth or fifth person to accept Islam in Mecca. He walked alone into Mecca to seek the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and boldly proclaimed the Shahada before Quraysh at the Kaaba. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ gave him the immortal tribute recorded in Sunan al-Tirmidhi: 'There is no one under the sky or above the earth more truthful in speech than Abu Dharr.'

quranic.note: Jandab is not in the Qur'an; its Islamic stature is established by authentic prophetic hadiths honoring Abu Dharr.

hadith_status.note: Celebrated in Jami' at-Tirmidhi (3801) and Sunan Ibn Majah (156) where the Prophet ﷺ declared Abu Dharr the most truthful of all people in speech.

names.morphology: Classical Arabic diminutive noun (pattern fuʿaylīl) from ʿaqaba, meaning 'the vigilant follower', 'careful guardian', or 'one who watches faithfully over trust'.
names.short_meaning: Vigilant guardian; trusted companion Muayqib ibn Abi Fatima, keeper of the Prophet's seal.
names.primary_meaning: Muayqib (مُعَيْقِيب) is an Arabic masculine given name meaning 'vigilant guardian', 'faithful keeper of trust', or 'steadfast successor'. In Islamic history, it is the renowned name of Muayqib ibn Abi Fatima ad-Dawsi, the trusted companion whom the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, Abu Bakr, and Umar appointed as the official custodian of the prophetic signet ring and the public treasury.
names.literal_meaning: Diminutive of ʿāqib (one who follows closely and guards with vigilant care), signifying trustworthiness, precision, and loyal oversight.
names.meaning_explanation: The root ʿ-q-b signifies following, guarding what comes after, and preserving trust. Muayqib embraced Islam early in Mecca, migrated to Abyssinia and then to Medina. Because of his scrupulous honesty, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ entrusted him with his personal signet ring (Khatam an-Nabi). Both Caliph Abu Bakr and Caliph Umar continued this absolute trust, making him overseer of the central treasury of the Caliphate.
names.semantic_domain: Trustworthiness, custody of the seal, treasury, companion name

quranic.note: Muayqib is not in the Qur'an; his historical role as custodian of the prophetic seal is documented in authentic Sunnah and historical chronicles.

hadith_status.note: Documented in Sahih al-Bukhari (5866) and Sahih Muslim (2091) regarding the custody and transmission of the Prophet's silver signet ring.

prophetic_status.note: Not the name of a prophet; belongs to an exceptionally trusted Companion.

companion_status.note: Muayqib ibn Abi Fatima ad-Dawsi (d. 40 AH / 660 CE), migrant to Abyssinia, keeper of the Prophet's seal, and treasurer of the early Caliphate.

names.name: Salit

names.short_meaning: Articulate, authoritative; early companion and prophetic envoy Salit ibn Amr.
names.primary_meaning: Salit (سَلِيط) is an Arabic masculine given name meaning 'eloquent, articulate, and commanding in speech' or 'clear-sighted authority'. In Islamic history, it is the renowned name of Salit ibn Amr al-Amiri, one of the earliest converts to Islam who migrated to Abyssinia, fought at Badr, and was selected by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ as his diplomatic envoy to the kingdom of Yamama.
names.literal_meaning: Derived from salāṭah (incisive eloquence and commanding clarity of tongue), denoting power of expression and persuasive intellect.
names.meaning_explanation: The root s-l-ṭ signifies authority, mastery, and articulate clarity. Salit ibn Amr was among the pioneers who embraced Islam in Mecca and suffered persecution. Because of his dignity, eloquence, and diplomatic poise, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ entrusted him with a historic letter to Hawdhah ibn Ali, the ruler of Yamama, calling him to Islam with wisdom and nobility.

quranic.note: The personal name Salit is not in the Qur'an; its root s-l-ṭ appears in the Quran in forms denoting authority and power (e.g. 4:90, 69:29).

hadith_status.note: Documented in Ibn Hisham's Sirah and Al-Isabah (Entry 3244) detailing his dispatch as the Prophet's envoy to Yamama.

names.name: Hubab
names.morphology: Classical Arabic substantive noun (pattern fuʿāl) denoting beloved affection, drops of clear morning dew, or the crest of pure water.
names.short_meaning: Beloved love, drops of dew; companion al-Hubab ibn al-Mundhir (Dhu al-Ra'y).
names.primary_meaning: Hubab (حُبَاب) is an authentic Arabic masculine given name meaning 'beloved affection', 'clear drops of morning dew', or 'the glistening surface of water'. In Islamic history, it is the renowned name of al-Hubab ibn al-Mundhir al-Ansari, known as 'Dhu al-Ra'y' (The Man of Sound Counsel) whose strategic military counsel at the Battle of Badr was embraced by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.
names.literal_meaning: Derived from ḥabb / ḥubb, signifying sweet affection, radiant dew on desert petals, or the crest of flowing water.
names.meaning_explanation: The root ḥ-b-b is the foundation of love and affection in Arabic. Al-Hubab ibn al-Mundhir was a veteran chieftain of the Khazraj. At the Battle of Badr, he politely inquired of the Prophet ﷺ whether the encampment location was divine revelation or human strategy. When told it was human strategy, Hubab suggested encamping at the closest well to the enemy and stopping up the rest, which the Prophet ﷺ praised and implemented immediately.
names.semantic_domain: Affection, strategic wisdom, Badr, companion name

quranic.note: Hubab does not occur as a proper name in the Qur'an; its triliteral root ḥ-b-b expresses divine love throughout the Qur'an (e.g. 2:165, 3:31).

hadith_status.note: His famous consultation with the Prophet ﷺ at Badr is recorded in Sunan al-Bayhaqi (Kitab al-Siyar) and Ibn Hisham's Sirah.

prophetic_status.note: Not the name of a prophet; belongs to an esteemed Ansari Companion.

companion_status.note: Al-Hubab ibn al-Mundhir al-Ansari (d. 20 AH / 641 CE), hero of Badr, Uhud, and the Trench, titled Dhu al-Ra'y for his brilliant tactical wisdom.

names.cultural_note: Celebrated in Islamic governance and military history as the supreme proof that Islam honors constructive consultation and expert analysis.
names.cultural_interpretation: Chosen to inspire loving kindness, intellectual brilliance, constructive initiative, and wise decision-making.

names.primary_meaning: Suwaybit (سُوَيْبِط) is an authentic Arabic masculine given name meaning 'flowing grace', 'generous nature', or 'smooth and gentle spirit'. In Islamic history, it is the renowned name of Suwaybit ibn Harmalah al-Qurashi, an early Meccan convert from Banu Abd al-Dar who migrated to Abyssinia and Medina, and fought at the Battle of Badr.
names.literal_meaning: Diminutive of sabiṭ (smooth, unknotted, flowing easily and generously), denoting good nature, openheartedness, and gentle kindness.
names.meaning_explanation: The root s-b-ṭ denotes flowing smoothly, generosity, and abundant ease. Suwaybit ibn Harmalah was among the early adherents of Islam in Mecca who endured persecution and joined the migration to Abyssinia. He was among the honored 313 warriors who stood at Badr with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, recognized for his cheerful demeanor and steadfast devotion.
